---
title: "Validation"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-validation
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: every example on this page uses `OrdersSchema` from `dd.data`"
#| output: false
import polars as pl

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely.data import OrdersSchema
```

With the default `filter=False`, a run of an asset built with `dd.asset` writes either every row the decorated function returns or nothing.
Which one it does depends on what the function returns and on the rules its rows fail.
Each rule has a severity, `"error"` or `"warn"` ([Rule severity](rule-severity.qmd)).

[Filtering error rows](filtering-error-rows.qmd) covers what `filter=True` changes.

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->
```{mermaid}
%%| label: validation-runs
flowchart TD
    F["the decorated function returns"] --> N{"None?"}
    N -- yes --> SKIP["skip: nothing written<br/>every check passes<br/>run succeeds"]
    N -- no --> CS{"column schema matches?"}
    CS -- no --> DRIFT["nothing written<br/>dy_schema__columns fails<br/>run fails, ColumnSchemaError"]
    CS -- yes --> FILTER["Schema.filter"]
    FILTER --> ERR{"a row failed an 'error' rule?"}
    ERR -- yes --> ABORT["nothing written<br/>each failing check has its rule's severity<br/>run fails, ValidationAbortError"]
    ERR -- no --> WRITE["every row written<br/>failing 'warn' checks at WARN<br/>run succeeds"]
```

A run writes nothing when the function returns `None`, when a column the schema declares is missing or has another dtype, or when a row fails an `"error"` rule.
Otherwise it writes every row, including the rows that failed only `"warn"` rules.

| what the function returned | the table | failing checks | run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a missing column, or a dtype that is not the schema's | not written | the column-schema check, blocking | fails, `ColumnSchemaError` |
| every row valid | written | none | succeeds |
| rows that failed only `"warn"` rules | written, including those rows | each `"warn"` rule's check, at `WARN` | succeeds |
| a row that failed an `"error"` rule | not written | each `"error"` rule's check at `ERROR`, each `"warn"` rule's check at `WARN` | fails, `ValidationAbortError` |
| `None`, meaning no source data | skipped | none | succeeds |

Each row of the table is one of the five kinds of run.
A failing check has its own rule's severity, even in a run that fails because of another rule.
When the column-schema check fails, its severity is always `ERROR`.

![The Checks tab of `finance_orders`, which has `filter=False`, after some rows failed an `"error"` rule. The selected check is blocking, and it failed.](../assets/images/severity-error.png)

![The run log shows the step failure. The `ValidationAbortError` message lists how many rows failed each `"error"` rule. The counts add up to more than the number of failing rows, because one row can fail several rules.](../assets/images/error-validation-abort.png)

**Every row has to pass every `"error"` rule.**
To write the error rows to a separate table and the other rows to the table, set `filter=True`.
To drop the failing rows yourself, drop them in the decorated function:

```{python}
#| label: validation-1
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    valid, _ = OrdersSchema.filter(raw_orders)
    return valid
```

`Schema.filter` also drops the rows that fail only `"warn"` rules.
The asset's checks then pass, because the package validates only the rows the function returns.

**A row that fails only `"warn"` rules is written.**
So the table satisfies every `"error"` rule, but not necessarily every `"warn"` rule.
An asset downstream that reads the table as `dy.DataFrame[OrdersSchema]` can rely only on the `"error"` rules.
The table has the valid rows first, then the rows that failed only `"warn"` rules, so it does not keep the frame's row order when a `"warn"` rule fails.

## The package never casts

The column-schema check compares your frame's dtypes with the schema's and fails the run on a mismatch.
`Schema.filter` runs with `cast=False`.
A dtype mismatch is a bug in the pipeline.
A silent cast can write wrong values.
For example, a cast from `Float64` to a declared `Int64` turns `1.9` into `1`, and every rule still passes.

The check reads only the frame's column schema, so it does not collect a `LazyFrame`.
It reports every mismatched column at once.

**Extra columns and column order are not a mismatch.**
The check compares only the columns the schema declares, and `Schema.filter` drops any other column.
The table has the schema's columns in the schema's order, whatever order the frame had:

```{python}
#| label: validation-2
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    # `raw_orders` has columns `OrdersSchema` does not declare, and `net` adds one more.
    return raw_orders.with_columns(net=pl.col("amount") * 0.8)
```

So a decorated function that returns extra columns needs no `select`, and no `Schema.cast` to drop them.

**To cast, call `Schema.cast` in the decorated function:**

```{python}
#| label: validation-3
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return OrdersSchema.cast(raw_orders)
```

A `Schema.cast` call in the decorated function is the intended way to cast, not a workaround.
Few assets need it.
An asset needs it when its source returns a dtype that differs from the schema's, most often on a read from a warehouse.
DuckDB returns a `DECIMAL` column, and a literal such as `1.5` in a query, as a Polars `Decimal`.
An asset whose schema declares `Float64` for such a column fails the column-schema check on every run unless it casts.
If you cast in every asset, check whether the dtypes differ at all ([#88](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/issues/88)).
